2|
3|> This is the document handed to candidates, together with the repository.
4|> (Interviewers: remove `docs/05-interviewer-guide.md` before sharing.)
5|
6|## Welcome to FairFahren 🚕
7|
8|You have a tiny 3D driving game: a Berlin taxi in a procedurally generated city. The whole game is about 50 KB of plain JavaScript — **no assets, no libraries, no build step**. Every building, tree and street comes from one seed number.
9|
10|Your job is to **extend it**.
11|
12|## Ground rules
13|
14|1. **Stay procedural.** Do not add image, model, audio, font or data files. Generate what you need in code.
15|2. **Stay small.** `npm run size` must pass (≤ 96 KB raw, ≤ 32 KB gzip for `index.html` + `src/`).
16|3. **No dependencies.** No npm packages, no CDN scripts — on the client and on any server you write.
17|4. **Stay deterministic.** World content must come from the seeded `Rng`, never from `Math.random()`.
18|5. **Keep it green.** `npm test` passes, and new logic comes with tests where it makes sense.
19|6. Small, focused commits with meaningful messages. We will read your history.
20|
21|## Getting started (≈ 30 min)
22|
23|1. Read [03-prerequisites.md](03-prerequisites.md), run `npm start`, drive around.
24|2. Read [02-technical-specification.md](02-technical-specification.md) and skim `src/main.js` — everything is wired there.
25|3. Try `?seed=7` and the `window.fairfahren` console object.
26|
27|## Tasks
28|
29|Pick **one main task** (or the one your interviewer gave you). Bonus tasks are optional.
30|
31|### A — Taxi missions (game loop) ★★
32|Turn the sandbox into a game. Spawn a waiting passenger (procedural figure + marker) at a random sidewalk spot, drive there and stop next to them to pick up, then deliver them to a destination shown on screen. Fare depends on distance and time; show money earned.
33|*Acceptance:* pickup only below 5 km/h within 4 m; destination reachable by road; fares and positions deterministic per seed + mission number; logic unit-tested without WebGL.
34|
35|### B — Traffic lights ★★
36|Add traffic lights at crossings (a pole with red/amber/green; bonus: the East-Berlin *Ampelmännchen* built from boxes). Cycle them per crossing so perpendicular directions never show green at the same time. Detect and display red-light violations.
37|*Acceptance:* state machine is a pure, tested module; lights are visible and readable at 50 m; violation is detected when crossing the stop line on red.
38|
39|### C — Minimap & navigation ★★★
40|Draw a minimap (2D canvas overlay) of streets, river and the taxi. Build a road graph from the city data and show the shortest route to a clicked destination (A* or Dijkstra).
41|*Acceptance:* the graph respects dead-ends at the river; route updates when the taxi leaves it; graph construction and pathfinding are tested.
42|
43|### D — AI traffic ★★★
44|Add 10–30 other cars that drive along the streets in the right-hand lane, turn at crossings and stop for obstacles in front of them (including the taxi).
45|*Acceptance:* no car drives through buildings or into the river; stays at ≥ 50 FPS; behaviour deterministic per seed.
46|
47|### E — A new district ★★
48|Add a new procedural block type with Berlin character — e.g. an elevated U-Bahn line (*Hochbahn*) on a viaduct along one street with stations, or a Kreuzberg-style street with *Spätis* and coloured awnings, or the Berlin Wall remnant with a strip of land.
49|*Acceptance:* integrated into `generateCity` via its own RNG fork; colliders where needed; invariant tests extended.
50|
51|### F — Better physics & feel ★★
52|Replace the kinematic model with a simple dynamic model: tyre slip, understeer/oversteer, handbrake drifts; body roll and pitch visible on the model; impact speed shakes the camera.
53|*Acceptance:* existing physics tests still pass or are consciously updated; new tests for slip behaviour.
54|
55|### G — Multiplayer race over the intranet ★★★★
56|Turn FairFahren into a short multiplayer race for **2–4 players** on different machines in the same network.
57|
58|**Flow**
59|
60|1. **Lobby.** One player starts the game server; the others open `http://<host-ip>:<port>/` and enter a name. Everyone sees who has joined (2–4 players, a fifth is turned away). Any player can press "Start" once at least two are in.
61|2. **Track.** A straight **200 m** race on a road of the city, e.g. eastwards along *Unter den Linden* from the gate. All clients derive the same track from the shared seed (the server picks the seed). Start grid with one slot per player, no taxi overlapping another.
62|3. **Start light (*Ampel*).** A traffic light above or beside the start line runs the German sequence **red → red + amber → green**. Cars are frozen until green. Every client must switch to green at the same moment (± 100 ms), regardless of network delay. Bonus: a jump start (moving before green) gets a time penalty.
63|4. **Race.** All players see all taxis moving in real time, smoothly, with a name tag. Each taxi is distinguishable (e.g. the player number on the roof sign or a coloured stripe — procedural, no textures).
64|5. **Finish line.** A visible chequered line across the road. Crossing it records the finish time (ms precision). The server, not the client, decides the official order.
65|6. **Siegerehrung.** When all players have finished (or 30 s after the winner), show the award ceremony to everyone: a podium with steps 1–2–3 built from geometry, the taxis placed on it, a camera orbit, and a results table with names and times. Then "Nochmal" returns everyone to the start grid.
66|
67|**Rules for this task**
68|
69|- The server is plain Node (`server/`), **zero dependencies** like the rest. Use the built-in `node:http`. You choose the transport — e.g. WebSocket via the HTTP `upgrade` handshake (RFC 6455, a few dozen lines), or Server-Sent Events plus `fetch` POSTs — and justify the choice in `NOTES.md`.
70|- The server serves the game files too, so players only need one URL. It listens on all network interfaces, not only `localhost`.
71|- The size budget still applies to the client (`index.html` + `src/`). Server code does not count.
72|- Single-player mode keeps working without a server.
73|
74|**Acceptance criteria**
75|
76|- Two browser windows on one machine **and** two machines in the intranet can race each other.
77|- The race state machine (lobby → countdown → racing → finished → ceremony) is a **pure module with unit tests**, including: start rejected with fewer than 2 players, fifth player rejected, finish order by time, a player disconnecting mid-race does not block the ceremony.
78|- The track (start grid, finish line) is generated from the seed and tested: 200 m long, straight, fully on road, no collider in the way.
79|- Other taxis move smoothly at 60 FPS even though network updates arrive at ~10–20 Hz (interpolation).
80|- The message protocol is documented (message types, fields, who sends what, at which rate).
81|
82|**Scoping.** This is the biggest task. In a time-boxed take-home, a solid result for steps 1–5 with two players beats a shaky all-in version; note in `NOTES.md` what you left out and how you would add it.
83|
84|### Bonus (small, any time)
85|- Headlights toggle (`L`) and a day/night cycle in the shader.
86|- Horn (WebAudio, synthesised — no audio files).
87|- Spatial grid for collision queries + a micro-benchmark.
88|- Gamepad support.
89|- Camera that does not clip into buildings.
90|
91|## What we look for
92|
93|Clean, readable code that fits the existing style; sensible decomposition (pure logic vs. rendering); tests for logic; respecting the constraints; and being able to **explain your trade-offs**. A smaller, solid result beats a large, fragile one.
94|
95|## Hand-in
96|
97|A Git repository (or bundle) with your commits, plus a short `NOTES.md`: what you built, what you'd do next, what you'd change in the existing code, how long you spent.", "total_lines": 97, "file_size": 7763, "truncated": false, "is_binary": false, "is_image": false, "not_found": false}

3|**Project:** FairFahren — procedural Berlin taxi driving simulation
4|**Purpose:** Prepared base project for developer interviews. Candidates extend it.
5|**Status:** MVP (v0.1.0)
6|
7|## 1. Vision
8|
9|A small 3D driving game in the browser: you steer a German taxi (light ivory, yellow "TAXI" roof sign) through a part of Berlin. Everything you see is **generated by code from a single seed**: no textures, no 3D models, no audio files. The whole game ships in **kilobytes, not megabytes**.
10|
11|The project is intentionally small, readable and dependency-free, so a candidate can understand it in 30–45 minutes and then extend it.
12|
13|## 2. Stakeholders
14|
15|| Role | Interest |
16||---|---|
17|| Hiring team / interviewers | A realistic, engaging task that reveals engineering skill: reading unfamiliar code, design, maths, performance, testing, communication. |
18|| Candidates | A fun, self-contained codebase that runs with zero setup friction. |
19|| Maintainers of the task | Easy to adjust difficulty, add new tasks, keep the reference solution in sync. |
20|
21|## 3. Functional requirements (MVP)
22|
23|| ID | Requirement | Acceptance criteria |
24||---|---|---|
25|| FR-01 | The game runs in a desktop browser from a static web server. | `npm start`, open `http://localhost:8080`, the city and taxi appear within 1 s. |
26|| FR-02 | The player drives a taxi with **W/A/S/D** or the **arrow keys**. | W/↑ accelerates, S/↓ brakes then reverses, A/← and D/→ steer. Works on QWERTY and QWERTZ. |
27|| FR-03 | Handbrake, reset and camera switching. | Space = handbrake, R = back to spawn, C cycles chase / bonnet / overhead camera. |
28|| FR-04 | The taxi looks like a German taxi. | Ivory saloon (RAL 1015 "Hellelfenbein"), yellow roof sign reading "TAXI" from front and back, turning and steering wheels. |
29|| FR-05 | The world is a procedurally generated part of Berlin. | Street grid with Berlin street names; perimeter blocks of pre-war buildings (*Altbau*) with courtyards; prefab panel buildings (*Plattenbau*), more of them to the east; parks; the river Spree with bridges; a boulevard "Unter den Linden" with linden trees; a city gate on the boulevard; a TV tower on a plaza. |
30|| FR-06 | The city is deterministic and seedable. | Same seed → identical city. `?seed=<int>` in the URL selects a different city. Default seed 1989. |
31|| FR-07 | The taxi collides with the world. | Cannot drive through buildings/curbs, gate pillars, river (except via bridges), or past the city border. Impacts bounce and slow the car. |
32|| FR-08 | HUD | Speed in km/h, current street name (or "A / B" on crossings, "… · Spreebrücke" on bridges), seed, FPS, camera mode, key help. |
33|
34|## 4. Non-functional requirements
35|
36|| ID | Requirement | Measure |
37||---|---|---|
38|| NFR-01 | **Size budget.** Shipped game (`index.html` + `src/**`) stays tiny. | ≤ 96 KB raw **and** ≤ 32 KB gzip, checked by `npm run size` (exit code 1 if exceeded). MVP: ~52 KB raw / ~19 KB gzip. |
39|| NFR-02 | **Fully procedural.** No binary or data assets. | No images, models, fonts, audio, JSON level files. Everything derived from code + seed. |
40|| NFR-03 | **Zero dependencies.** | No runtime or dev npm dependencies; no CDN scripts. Node is only needed for the dev server, tests and size check. |
41|| NFR-04 | **Performance.** | 60 FPS on a mid-range laptop with integrated GPU at 1080p. City = one draw call. Generation < 50 ms. |
42|| NFR-05 | **Determinism.** | World generation uses only the seeded RNG (never `Math.random()`); physics runs at a fixed 120 Hz step. |
43|| NFR-06 | **Testability.** | World generation, physics and collision are pure modules (no DOM/WebGL) with unit tests (`npm test`). |
44|| NFR-07 | **Readability.** | Plain modern JavaScript (ES2022 modules), no build step, short files with a header comment explaining purpose. |
45|| NFR-08 | **Browser support.** | Current Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari with WebGL2. Clear error message if WebGL2 is missing. |
46|
47|## 5. Out of scope for the MVP
48|
49|These are deliberately left out and are good candidate tasks (see [04-candidate-brief.md](04-candidate-brief.md)):
50|passengers / fares / game loop, traffic & pedestrians, traffic lights, minimap, sound, day/night, shadows, mobile/touch/gamepad controls, infinite or streamed city, damage, save games, multiplayer races over the intranet (task G).
51|
52|## 6. Constraints and assumptions
53|
54|- Must run offline after checkout — no network access needed.
55|- Interview sessions are 2–4 h (take-home) or 60–90 min (live pairing); tasks are sized accordingly.
56|- Berlin is represented by recognisable *character* (block structure, river, boulevard, landmarks, names), not by an accurate map.
57|- Landmarks are generic stylised shapes, not reproductions of copyrighted designs.
58|

60|

64|| Berliner Block | Large urban block with perimeter buildings around inner courtyards (*Hinterhöfe*). |
65|| Plattenbau | Prefab concrete-panel housing (GDR era), 8–11 floors. |
66|| Baulücke | Vacant lot in an otherwise closed row of buildings. |
67|| Ufer | Riverside street ("bank"), e.g. *Reichpietschufer*. |

{"content": "1|# 02 — Technical specification
2|
3|## 1. Architecture overview
4|
5|```
6|                 seed (4 bytes)
7|                      │
8|                      ▼
9|   ┌──────────── world/cityGen.js ─────────────┐   pure data, runs in Node
10|   │ streets, blocks, buildings, river,        │
11|   │ trees, landmarks, markings, colliders     │
12|   └───────┬───────────────────────┬───────────┘
13|           │                       │
14|           ▼                       ▼
15|   world/cityMesh.js        vehicle/collision.js ◄── vehicle/carPhysics.js ◄── game/input.js
16|   (data → triangles)              │                        │
17|           │                       └──────────┬─────────────┘
18|           ▼                                  ▼
19|   gfx/meshBuilder.js ──► gfx/renderer.js ◄── game/camera.js
20|                               │
21|                         gfx/shaders.js  (procedural surface detail)
22|```
23|
24|Rule of the codebase: **data in, data out.** Generation and simulation never touch the DOM or WebGL; rendering never decides game logic. `main.js` is the only place that wires everything together.
25|
26|## 2. Module reference
27|
28|| File | Responsibility | Pure? |
29||---|---|---|
30|| `src/main.js` | Bootstraps everything, fixed-timestep game loop, HUD updates. | no |
31|| `src/core/rng.js` | Seeded PRNG (mulberry32), string hashing, forkable streams. | yes |
32|| `src/core/math.js` | `clamp/lerp/damp/approach`, 4×4 matrices (column-major). | yes |
33|| `src/gfx/meshBuilder.js` | CPU-side geometry: `poly`, `rect`, `box`, `frustum`, `cylinderX`, `sphere`. Auto-orients faces. | yes |
34|| `src/gfx/shaders.js` | One GLSL ES 3.0 program; procedural windows, water, asphalt, soft shadow. | – |
35|| `src/gfx/renderer.js` | WebGL2 context, mesh upload (VAO), per-frame uniforms, draw calls. | no |
36|| `src/world/cityGen.js` | Procedural city as plain data + `streetAt()` lookup. | yes |
37|| `src/world/cityMesh.js` | Converts city data into one static mesh. | yes |
38|| `src/vehicle/carPhysics.js` | `TAXI` tuning, `createCar`, `stepCar` (bicycle model). | yes |
39|| `src/vehicle/collision.js` | `pushOut` (circle vs boxes/circles), `collideCar` (response). | yes |
40|| `src/vehicle/taxiModel.js` | Taxi body, wheel and shadow meshes; wheel positions. | yes |
41|| `src/game/input.js` | Keyboard state, edge-triggered presses, driving input mapping. | no |
42|| `src/game/camera.js` | Chase / bonnet / overhead rigs with smoothing. | yes* |
43|| `src/game/hud.js` | Writes HUD text only when it changes. | no |
44|
45|\* no DOM, but only used by the browser.
46|
47|## 3. Conventions
48|
49|- **Coordinates:** Y up, **X east, Z south**, metres. Heading 0 faces +Z; forward = `(sin h, 0, cos h)`; positive heading/steer = left turn.
50|- **Matrices:** column-major `Float32Array(16)`, `compose(a, b, c) = a·b·c`.
51|- **Colors:** data stores `0xRRGGBB` ints; mesh code converts with `rgb()`.
52|- **Randomness:** only via `Rng`. Every feature uses its own `rng.fork('label')`; every block uses `fork('block:x,z')`. Adding random calls in one feature therefore does **not** change the rest of the city.
53|
54|## 4. City generation (`generateCity(options)`)
55|
56|Config defaults (`DEFAULT_CITY`): 8×7 blocks of 70–105 m, streets 14 m, boulevard 36 m with an 8 m median, river 46 m, sidewalks 4 m, curb 0.15 m.
57|
58|Steps:
59|
60|1. **Special rows.** Pick the river row (southern half) and the boulevard street (north of the river).
61|2. **Axis layout.** Alternate streets and blocks along X and Z (`layoutAxis`), centred on the origin. The river row has a fixed width; the boulevard is wider.
62|3. **Names.** Shuffle pools of real Berlin street names; boulevard = *Unter den Linden*, river banks get *-ufer/-damm* names.
63|4. **River & bridges.** Each N–S street crosses the Spree with probability 0.6; two streets always do.
64|5. **Landmarks.** City gate mid-block on the boulevard in column 1 (six pillar pairs, five drivable passages). TV tower on a plaza block east of centre.
65|6. **Blocks.** Kind per block: plaza (fixed), park (*Tiergarten* next to the gate, else 10 %), *Plattenbau* (18 % rising to 53 % in the east), else *Altbau*.
66|   - *Altbau:* perimeter rows of 12–16 m depth around a courtyard, split into 12–22 m parcels (no slivers < 10 m), 4–6 floors × 3.6 m, 75 % gable roofs, 6 % vacant lots, 0–2 courtyard trees.
67|   - *Plattenbau:* 1–2 slabs, 12 m deep, along the longer block side, 8–11 floors × 2.8 m, trees on the lawn.
68|   - *Park:* trees scattered with 6 m minimum spacing (≈ 1 per 220 m²).
69|7. **Median** with linden trees every 11 m, gaps at crossings and ±14 m around the gate.
70|8. **Markings** as line segments (dashed by the mesh builder): centre lines; two lane dividers on the boulevard.
71|9. **Forest** ring around the city (260 attempts).
72|10. **Colliders** (`{type:'box'|'circle', …, tag}`): every block (curb), medians, gate pillar walls, river segments between bridges, four border walls.
73|11. **Spawn**: right-hand lane of the boulevard, 30 m east of the gate, heading east.
74|
75|Output shape (abridged):
76|
77|```js
78|{ seed, config, bounds:{x0,z0,x1,z1},
79|  streetsNS:[{center,width,kind,name}], streetsEW:[…],
80|  river:{name,z0,z1,bridges:[{street,x0,x1}]},
81|  blocks:[{ix,iz,x0,z0,x1,z1,kind,ground,buildings:[{kind,x0,z0,x1,z1,y0,height,color,roof,roofColor,roofHeight,ridgeAlongX}]}],
82|  medians, markings:[{x0,z0,x1,z1}], trees:[{x,y,z,s}],
83|  landmarks:[{kind:'gate',x,z,width,pillars}, {kind:'tvTower',x,y,z}],
84|  colliders:[…], spawn:{x,z,heading} }
85|```
86|
87|## 5. Rendering
88|
89|- **WebGL2**, one shader program. Vertex format: position(3) normal(3) color(3) material(1) = 40 bytes.
90|- **Flat shading**: every face has its own vertices and normal → low-poly look, no smoothing groups.
91|- **Face orientation**: `MeshBuilder.poly()` computes the normal with Newell's method and flips it (and the winding) away from a given interior point, so back-face culling just works.
92|- **Materials** (`MAT`): `PLAIN`, `ALTBAU`, `PLATTE` (window grids from world position, shop fronts on the ground floor, panel joints), `WATER` (animated normal + specular), `ASPHALT` (grain), `PAINT` (specular), `SHADOW` (radial alpha from uv in the color slot).
93|- **Lighting**: Lambert sun + hemispheric sky/ground ambient + Blinn-Phong for glossy materials + fake ambient occlusion at wall bases + exp² distance fog that hides the world edge.
94|- **Draw calls per frame**: city (1), taxi body (1), wheels (4), shadow (1, blended).
95|- Typical city (seed 1989): ~450 buildings, ~520 trees → ~87 k vertices / ~40 k triangles (≈ 3.5 MB GPU memory). Data generation ≈ 3 ms, mesh building ≈ 20 ms (Node, laptop).
96|
97|## 6. Vehicle physics (`stepCar`)
98|
99|Kinematic bicycle model, fixed step 1/120 s:
100|
101|- Steering approaches `input.steer × limit` at `steerRate`. The limit is grip-based: `min(maxSteer, atan(maxLateralAccel·L / v²))`.
102|- Longitudinal: throttle accelerates (fading to 0 at `maxSpeed`) or brakes when rolling backwards; brake pedal brakes, then reverses up to `maxReverse`.
103|- Resistances: rolling + quadratic air drag (+ handbrake); never flip the direction of travel.
104|- Yaw rate `v / L · tan(δ)` (× 1.4 with handbrake), then integrate position and wheel spin.
105|
106|## 7. Collision (`collideCar`)
107|
108|- Car = two circles (r 0.95 m) at ±1.45 m along the car axis.
109|- `pushOut` resolves the circle against all colliders one after the other (closest-point test for boxes, nearest-side exit if the centre is inside).
110|- Response: reflect the velocity component along the contact normal with restitution 0.25, project back onto the car axis. Returns the impact speed (unused in the MVP — hook for damage/sound).
111|- Broad phase: none (≈ 75 colliders, cheap bounding-box reject first). A spatial grid is a natural extension.
112|
113|## 8. Size budget enforcement
114|
115|`tools/size-check.mjs` concatenates `index.html` and every file in `src/`, measures raw and gzip-9 size, prints a per-file table and fails above **96 KB raw / 32 KB gzip**. `npm run check` = tests + size. Tests, docs and tools are not shipped and do not count.
116|
117|## 9. Testing
118|
119|`node --test` (built in, no dependencies). Covered: RNG determinism and ranges; city determinism, world invariants for several seeds (buildings within blocks, no blocks in the river, ≥ 2 bridges, exactly one of each landmark, collision-free spawn on *Unter den Linden*); physics (acceleration, top speed, braking/reversing, coasting to a stop, steering direction, wall collision, bounce).
120|
121|Rendering is verified manually; `window.fairfahren` exposes `{ city, car, camera, TAXI }` for console inspection.", "total_lines": 121, "file_size": 8691, "truncated": false, "is_binary": false, "is_image": false, "not_found": false}

{"content": "1|# G — Multiplayer race: brainstorm (questions to answer before planning)
2|
3|Task: **G — Multiplayer race over the intranet** (`docs/04-candidate-brief.md`).
4|This is a working document: the questions we must answer, with "for dummies"
5|explanations, pros/cons, and a recommendation for each. No decisions are final
6|until the plan (02-plan.md) records them.
7|
8|## How to read this
9|
10|For each open question: what the question means in plain words, the realistic
11|options, what each costs/gains, and what we'd recommend — plus why.
12|
13|---
14|
15|## Q1 — Transport: how do the server and browsers talk?
16|
17|The browser can't just "call" the server whenever it wants in both directions.
18|HTTP is like asking a question and getting an answer — every reactive bit

## The big picture first

Task G turns the solo taxi sandbox into a **2–4 player race on a local network**. That means four new kinds of problems:

1. **How do machines talk to each other?** (Q1)
2. **Who's the boss when players disagree?** (Q2, Q3)
3. **How do other cars look smooth?** (Q4, Q13)
4. **How do we keep it testable, small, and not break solo mode?** (Q5–Q12, Q14–Q15)

## Q1 — How do the browser and server talk?

Browsers can't just "call" the server any time. Normal HTTP is like **asking a question and waiting for the answer** — every time the server wants to push "the other taxi moved", it can't, unless we open a special channel.

**Option A — Hand-rolled WebSocket.** A "phone call" that stays open: both sides talk whenever they want, with tiny message overhead.
- ✅ Both directions, constant, cheap — perfect for positions at 10–20×/second.
- ✅ The brief suggests it (a few dozen lines: the handshake + message framing).
- ❌ We write the protocol plumbing ourselves (SHA-1 handshake key, frame masking). Trickiest code in the project.

**Option B — Server-Sent Events + POSTs.** A "radio broadcast" (server → you) plus "letters mailed back" (you → server via HTTP POST).
- ✅ Almost zero protocol code — it's just HTTP.
- ❌ Every player input is a brand-new HTTP request — clunky and laggy for a real-time race.

👉 **Recommend: A (WebSocket).** One phone line beats a radio + a stack of letters.

## Q2 — Who is the boss? (authority model)

Someone needs the final say on who joined, when the light goes green, and who finished first.

**Option A — Clients simulate their own car; server relays positions and owns the rules.** Your taxi still runs on the physics the game already has (120 Hz, deterministic). You broadcast "I'm here, facing this way, going this fast" ~15×/second. The server just forwards these **and** owns the game rules (lobby, green light, finish order, podium).
- ✅ Physics code already exists and is already tested — we barely touch it.
- ✅ No "two simulators fighting over one car" problem (the classic netcode swamp).
- ❌ We trust what players report — a cheat could lie. (Impossible to fix in scope; out of scope is fine.)

**Option B — Server simulates everyone's car.** Perfectly fair, one truth.
- ❌ Needs client prediction + reconciliation of 120 Hz physics. This alone can eat the whole budget. Too big here.

**Option C — Server is just a dumb pipe.** Forwards everything, knows nothing.
- ❌ The brief *requires* the server to run the lobby and decide the official finish order. A dumb pipe can't.

👉 **Recommend: A.** The server owns the *rules*, clients own their own wheels — exactly like solo mode today.

## Q3 — Four different computers, four different clocks — how do they agree on "now"?

The brief says every screen shows **green at the same moment ±100 ms**, and finishes are timed to the millisecond. One laptop's clock might be minutes off from another's.

**Option A — Server = master clock, measured with pings.** Client asks "what time is it?" repeatedly, measures the round-trip, and works out the offset (like calling the speaking clock and noting how long the answer took). Then everyone counts down to the same server timestamp.
- ✅ Simple, and the 100 ms tolerance is huge compared to a home-network delay of 1–5 ms.
- ✅ Same trick timestamps the finish: report "I crossed at server-time T", server sorts by T.

**Option B — Server just broadcasts "GO now" on receipt.**
- ✅ No clock math.
- ❌ Whoever's message arrives last starts last. Doesn't meet the ±100 ms rule.

**Option C — Broadcast a 3-2-1 countdown.**
- ✅ Humans forgive slow countdowns.
- ❌ Still not millisecond-grade; more protocol noise.

👉 **Recommend: A**, pinging continuously while everyone is parked in the lobby so the offset is solid before the countdown. GO = one shared server timestamp.

## Q4 — Remote taxis: smooth at 60 FPS while updates arrive at ~15 Hz

Showing only the latest received position makes other cars **jump** 15 times a second.

**Option A — Buffer + interpolate.** Keep the last few snapshots and render *between* them, with a small (~100 ms) delay — like watching a live sports broadcast: it's a bit behind real time, but buttery.
- ✅ Simple math (lerp position, nudge heading), easy to unit test.
- ❌ A constant ~100 ms visual delay on other cars — invisible here (200 m straight race, fairness unaffected).

**Option B — Dead reckoning.** *Predict* where the car will be: "he's going 60 km/h east, so next frame he'll be a bit further east."
- ✅ Lower perceived lag.
- ❌ Wrong guesses show as rubber-banding; each fix branch adds risk.

👉 **Recommend: A.** On a straight 200 m track, 100 ms of visual lag doesn't matter; prediction's edge cases do.

## Q5 — The race state machine (lobby → countdown → racing → finished → ceremony)

This is the brief's hard requirement: **pure module with unit tests**, including "start refused with < 2 players", "5th player turned away", "a disconnected player doesn't block the ceremony".

- Pure module `raceState`: roster + stage in, decisions out. No DOM, no network.
- Thin server wrapper that feeds real sockets into it. Thin client that displays its output.
- ✅ Every acceptance rule becomes a plain unit test.

One sub-decision: the client *displays* the server's stage rather than running a second copy of the machine (two copies = two chances to disagree).

## Q6 — Where does the 200 m track come from?

All clients must derive the **same track from the same seed**: a straight 200 m road, start grid slots (cars not overlapping), finish line, nothing in the way.

- **A — The boulevard *Unter den Linden* east of the gate.** Guaranteed long, wide, straight; it's already the spawn road.
- **B — Search any street generically** for 200 m clear.

👉 **Recommend: A**, but write it as a *validated* pure function whose invariants (200 m, on road, no collider blocking) are tested — so it still holds even if city generation changes later.

## Q7 — Do taxis bump into each other?

- **Pass-through (ghost cars):** cheap, fair, no extra message protocol between cars.
- **Bumping:** feels more real, but "whose simulation decides where both cars end up" is a whole protocol of its own.

👉 **Recommend: pass-through** for the solid core; document bumping as the next step. (The only overlap rule the brief demands — grid slots — is solved by placement, not physics.)

## Q8 — Solo mode must keep working; one URL for everyone

- Solo (`npm start`) must keep working exactly as today.
- The race server also serves the game files, so players only need one URL. `tools/serve.mjs` (23 lines, `node:http`) grows into `server/` — the static-serving part gets extracted, no copy-paste.
- Client net code only activates when a multiplayer flag/flow says so.

## Q9 — Size budget

Budget: ≤ 96 KB raw / ≤ 32 KB gzip for `index.html` + `src/` (server code is free). MVP is ~52 KB raw — roughly 87 KB cost per 1 KB of headroom-used math aside, that's ~44 KB of room. Lobby UI + clock + interpolation + remote cars + podium ≈ **15–25 KB raw** estimated. ✔ fits, but we run `npm run size` early and often, not at the end.

## Q10 — Testing multiplayer without a network

No browsers in unit tests. So:
- Pure modules everywhere: state machine, WS frame codec, clock math, interpolation, track picker.
- An **in-memory fake network** (`FakeServer` + `FakeConnection` pairs with scripted timestamps) to test whole flows — two players join, countdown, finish order, disconnect mid-race — with zero sockets.

## Q11 — What can get cut if time runs out?

- **Must:** lobby + server, 2–4 cap, grid, green light ±100 ms, positions ~15 Hz, smooth remote cars, finish line + server-ordered times, tested track.
- **Should:** jump-start penalty, name tags/colours, podium *steps*.
- **Could:** orbit camera, "Nochmal" loop.
- **Won't:** taxi bumping, cheat protection, internet (non-LAN) play — all documented in `NOTES.md`.

## Q12 — Edge cases to decide up front

- Player disconnects mid-race → marked DNF, race continues, ceremony still happens.
- Two tabs, one machine → identity = connection ID + name, fine.
- Server crash mid-race → out of scope, documented.

---

## New questions added today (Q13–15)

**Q13 — How do we draw the *other* players' taxis?** One remote taxi ≈ 6 draw calls (body + 4 wheels + shadow), so up to ~18 extra draws for 4 players. Re-draw the existing taxi mesh with a different transform/costume (✅ nearly zero code; ❌ tiny renderer change) vs. rebuild merged geometry every frame (✅ fewer draws; ❌ wasteful CPU). 👉 Recommend re-drawing — 18 draw calls is nothing next to the city's 87k vertices. Still open for the plan: proving player number/colour via shader uniform or mesh variant, and name tags.

**Q14 — The seed mismatch.** A player's browser loads the game and generates a city *before* they even know the race seed — so at some point they must throw that city away and regenerate from the server's seed. Regeneration takes ~23 ms, so it's a blink, but we must pick the moment. 👉 Recommend: seed assigned in the lobby; each client regenerates on join ("Warming up…"), *before* any racing. Open for the plan: does "Nochmal" re-roll the seed (fresh city) or reuse it (instant restart)?

**Q15 — Protocol documentation is a required deliverable.** A `type | from | fields | rate` table in `NOTES.md`, written from the code (the pure protocol module), not invented beforehand.

| 2 | Authority | Server owns rules + relays; clients own their car physics |
| 3 | Clocks | Server master clock + pings; GO = one shared timestamp |
| 4 | Remote smoothing | Interpolation with ~100 ms buffer |
| 5 | State machine | Pure module + unit tests, sockets injected around it |
| 6 | Track | Unter den Linden, validated by invariant tests |
| 7 | Car vs car | Ghosts; bumping documented as future work |
| 8 | Solo compatibility | Solo untouched; net mode opt-in |
| 9 | Size budget | Additive `src/net/`, size-checked continuously |
| 10 | Testing | Pure modules + in-memory fake network |
| 11 | Scope | Solid 2-player core; podium second; WAN never |
| 12 | Edge cases | Disconnect = DNF; server restart out of scope |
| 13 | Remote rendering | Re-draw same taximesh with new transform |
| 14 | Seed sync | Server seed at lobby; regenerate before racing |
| 15 | Protocol doc | Table in NOTES.md from the code |

I've added a "Manual testing per phase" section to `docs/plans/g-multiplayer/02-plan.md`. Here's the gist, in for-dummies style:

## Phase 1 (server + WebSocket pipe) — "does the door open?"
- Open `http://localhost:8080` in **two tabs** (server running via `node server/main.mjs`) — the game must load and drive exactly like `npm start` did.
- Grab your PC's IP (`ipconfig`, IPv4 address), open `http://<that-ip>:8080` on another device in the same Wi-Fi — it must also load. That proves "listens on all interfaces".
- Test the handshake itself with curl in a terminal (it's like shaking the WebSocket's hand without using a browser): send the RFC's example key, and the server must answer `HTTP/1.1 101` with the expected `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value listed in the plan.

## Phase 2 (pure game rules) — "almost no manual testing, on purpose"
- The point of this phase is everything runs in `npm test` — no browser needed.
- For a real-socket smoke test, we keep a tiny throwaway "fake player" script (`node tools/smokeClient.mjs <name>`): it connects to the real server and behaves like a player. Start the server plus **two smoke players in two terminals** and watch the story unfold: roster appears → start refused with one player → accepted with two → positions flow → finishes ordered → podium announced even if one player "disconnects".

## Phase 3 (lobby + seeing each other) — first time you *see* multiplayer
Two browser windows side by side (Win+← / Win+→):
1. Join as "A" in one, "B" in the other → both rosters show both names.
2. Same city: identical street name + seed on both HUDs.
3. Drive in window A → window B shows your taxi moving **smoothly** (HUD FPS ≥ 60). The ~100 ms visual delay should feel invisible — smoothness is the one thing unit tests can't judge, so this is the moment to eyeball it.
4. Close a tab and rejoin → back in the lobby, roster updates everywhere.
5. Open a **fifth** tab → it gets shown the "full" turn-away screen.

## Phase 4 (the race itself) — full run-through
1. Both tabs on the grid → press Start → ampel runs red → red+amber → green; both windows turn green at the same time (the maths is unit-tested; your eyes check there's no visible skew).
2. Tap W *just before* green → that player gets a jump-start penalty.
3. Race to the chequered line → results table, podium, order matches reality.
4. "Nochmal" → everyone back on the grid for round two.
5. Close one tab mid-race → race still finishes, that player shows as DNF on the podium.
6. Once, on two separate machines, do the whole dance.
7. **Regression check:** plain `npm start` (no race server) must still spawn and drive exactly as it did before any of this.
